None of the three solutions is convincingly derived, so I can only give a tentative pick. I could not check the literature or run any computation here.

- **Solution 1 ($w_{\max}=q$)** rests on a dimension recurrence $d(w)=d(w-1)+d(w-q)$ that is asserted, not derived. Its $q=2$ check depends on that unsupported recurrence, so it gives no real evidence.
- **Solution 3 ($w_{\max}=q-1$)** claims an $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear relation at weight $q$ involving $\zeta(q)$ and $\zeta(q-1,1)$. It offers no explicit identity. The known weight-$q$ relation, $\zeta(q)=(T-T^q)\,\zeta(1,q-1)$, has coefficients in $K=\mathbb{F}_q(T)$, not $\mathbb{F}_q$, so it does not by itself break $\mathbb{F}_q$-independence.
- **Solution 2 ($w_{\max}=2q$)** is the only one with a concrete mechanism. It locates the first failure in a product identity, $\zeta(1,q)\,\zeta(1,q-1)=(\zeta(1,1,q-1)+\zeta(2,q-1))\,\zeta(q)$, whose two sides expand into weight-$(2q+1)$ MZVs with $\mathbb{F}_p$ coefficients. A nontrivial relation from that is plausible. Its $q=2$ example at weight 5 is checkable in principle but I have not verified it. Its weight-$q$ and $(q+1)$ statements are consistent with the known $K$-linear relations, and it correctly separates $K$-linear from $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear relations.

Solution 2 is the most credible of the three, but I have not confirmed the value $2q$ against the literature, so treat this as a tentative choice.

CHOICE: 2
